Well, mood... let me think about that. You know, people ask me how I am, and emotionally speaking, I feel just exactly like I always have. I wouldn't say I've had any real changes in my mood, no. I mean, I’m certainly not walking around on cloud nine or feeling unusually joyful. My friend Martha, bless her heart, she started taking some new medication for her joints a few months ago, and suddenly she was just giddy all the time, laughing at the absolute drop of a hat—but that is certainly not me. I’m just... normal, I suppose. 

And as for being irritable, well, I get a little frustrated sometimes, sure, but who wouldn't when they drop a whole tin of sewing buttons on the floor because their hands just won't stay still? Or when I can't get a thread through a needle because I'm rushing? But irritable in general at other people? No, not really. I'm quite content. I love seeing my grandchildren, I enjoy my garden... it's not a feeling of being unusually happy or having this grand, euphoric energy in my mind. It's really just this... physical need to be doing something. 

I remember telling my daughter, Susan, just last week when she came over for tea. I was up and down from the table four times before she even finished her first cup, and I said to her, "Susan, I feel perfectly fine in my head, I'm not upset, I'm not overly excited, I just need to wipe down these baseboards right this very second." So, no, doctor, I wouldn't say my mood is any different than it was ten or twenty years ago. My spirits are perfectly level. It's just my body that seems to think we're running a marathon!

Memory... well, now that you ask, no, I really haven't noticed anything out of the ordinary with my memory. I mean, goodness, at 87, you expect a little slippage here and there, don't you? It's just that... well, sometimes when people are talking, especially if they talk very slowly or take a long time to get to the point, I just want them to hurry up! I find myself nodding along, saying "Yes, yes, go on," because my hands are itching to get back to whatever project I was working on. Just yesterday, my neighbor Mr. Henderson was telling me about his new sprinkler system, and he was going into all this detail about the water pressure and the timer settings, and I understood every word of it, I really did, but I was practically bouncing on my heels because I knew I still had two dozen cookies to frost for the bake sale. I didn't lose the thread of the conversation, I just... I just wanted it to be over so I could get back to doing things! So no, my memory and my thinking are just fine. It's just this constant, buzzing need to be busy that's the problem.

Changes in my personality? Oh, heavens no. I mean, I am exactly the same person I have always been. I still see my friends, we still have our weekly canasta games on Thursday afternoons—though, as I was saying earlier, I do tend to pop up and down to refill the mixed nuts and the iced tea a bit more than the other ladies do. I just couldn't stop my hand from going up because I felt that overwhelming physical urge to take on another project. But it wasn't a thoughtless act, if that makes sense. I wasn't out of my mind or acting out of character. 

My daughter Susan, she did tell me just the other day that I am going to wear myself down to the bone, but she didn't say my personality had changed. She knows I've always liked a tidy house and a full schedule, ever since she was a little girl. It's just the sheer volume of the pacing and the fixing lately that's exhausting me. I'm not going out and buying things I don't need or acting wildly. I've lived in my house for forty-two years, and I've always prided myself on being a thoughtful, deliberate neighbor. 

Like just last week, Mrs. Gable across the street—she is a lovely woman, a bit frail now, uses one of those aluminum walkers—she had a heavy package left right on the edge of her driveway by the delivery man. I saw it from my kitchen window and immediately went out to carry it up to her porch. Now, I practically power-walked over there because my legs just needed to move, and I probably shouldn't have been lifting something that heavy at my age, but it wasn't impulsive in a careless way. It was just me being helpful while also needing to burn off that energy. So no, doctor, no real changes in who I am or how I treat people, just... just this endless motor keeping me on my feet.

It's really just this... physical need to be doing something. \n\nI remember telling my daughter, Susan, just last week when she came over for tea. I was up and down from the table four times before she even finished her first cup, and I said to her, \"Susan, I feel perfectly fine in my head, I'm not upset, I'm not overly excited, I just need to wipe down these baseboards right this very second.\" So, no, doctor, I wouldn't say my mood is any different than it was ten or twenty years ago. My spirits are perfectly level. It's just my body that seems to think we're running a marathon!\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your memory or thinking over this past year? For example, do you sometimes forget things you normally wouldn't, or do you find it harder to concentrate or follow conversations?\n\nPatient: Memory... well, now that you ask, no, I really haven't noticed anything out of the ordinary with my memory. I mean, goodness, at 87, you expect a little slippage here and there, don't you? My friend Helen—she's 89, bless her—she can't remember where she put her glasses half the time, and they're usually sitting right on top of her head! But me? No, my mind is sharp as a tack. I can tell you exactly what I wore to my high school graduation, and I can tell you what I had for breakfast this morning—oatmeal with half a sliced banana and just a sprinkle of cinnamon, by the way. I never forget a birthday, either. I have three children, eight grandchildren, and four great-grandchildren, and I send a card for every single one of them, right on time. I even remember to put the little return address labels on the envelopes, the ones with the little bluebirds on them that I ordered from that catalog last spring. \n\nAs for concentrating or following conversations, well, I don't have any trouble understanding what people are saying, not at all. My hearing is still quite good, thankfully. It's just that... well, sometimes when people are talking, especially if they talk very slowly or take a long time to get to the point, I just want them to hurry up! I find myself nodding along, saying \"Yes, yes, go on,\" because my hands are itching to get back to whatever project I was working on. Just yesterday, my neighbor Mr. Henderson was telling me about his new sprinkler system, and he was going into all this detail about the water pressure and the timer settings, and I understood every word of it, I really did, but I was practically bouncing on my heels because I knew I still had two dozen cookies to frost for the bake sale. I didn't lose the thread of the conversation, I just... I just wanted it to be over so I could get back to doing things! So no, my memory and my thinking are just fine. It's just this constant, buzzing need to be busy that's the problem.\n\nDoctor: Over this past year, have you noticed any changes in how you interact with people, or has anyone commented that you seem different in your personality or behavior—perhaps more impulsive, or doing things you wouldn't normally do before thinking them through?\n\nPatient: Changes in my personality? Oh, heavens no. I mean, I am exactly the same person I have always been. I still see my friends, we still have our weekly canasta games on Thursday afternoons—though, as I was saying earlier, I do tend to pop up and down to refill the mixed nuts and the iced tea a bit more than the other ladies do. But they certainly haven't said I seem different as a person or anything like that. \n\nAnd as for doing things without thinking them through, or being impulsive... well, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, it depends on what you mean by impulsive, I suppose. If you mean going out and making rash decisions, or saying rude things to people, absolutely not. I still have all my manners, thank goodness! When I signed up for that library committee I told you about, I knew exactly what it entailed, and I knew I was already tired. I just... I just couldn't stop my hand from going up because I felt that overwhelming physical urge to take on another project. But it wasn't a thoughtless act, if that makes sense. I wasn't out of my mind or acting out of character. \n\nMy daughter Susan, she did tell me just the other day that I am going to wear myself down to the bone, but she didn't say my personality had changed. She knows I've always liked a tidy house and a full schedule, ever since she was a little girl. It's just the sheer volume of the pacing and the fixing lately that's exhausting me. I'm not going out and buying things I don't need or acting wildly. I've lived in my house for forty-two years, and I've always prided myself on being a thoughtful, deliberate neighbor. \n\nLike just last week, Mrs. Gable across the street—she is a lovely woman, a bit frail now, uses one of those aluminum walkers—she had a heavy package left right on the edge of her driveway by the delivery man. I saw it from my kitchen window and immediately went out to carry it up to her porch. Now, I practically power-walked over there because my legs just needed to move, and I probably shouldn't have been lifting something that heavy at my age, but it wasn't impulsive in a careless way. It was just me being helpful while also needing to burn off that energy. So no, doctor, no real changes in who I am or how I treat people, just... just this endless motor keeping me on my feet.\n\n[Last Question]\nHave you noticed any difficulty finding the right words when you're speaking, or has anyone mentioned that your speech sounds different or that you're having trouble understanding certain types of words or instructions?\n\n[Patient Info]\n- demographics: Female / 87 / not_in_workforce / some_college\n- severity: Mild\n\n[Targeted Info]\nNone\n\n[Conversation Style]\nYou are a Verbose patient.\nA verbose patient may\n1) provide excessively detailed responses when describing their symptoms and experiences, even when the details are directly relevant,\n2) elaborate extensively on the background, events, thoughts, feelings, and personal experiences surrounding their symptoms, and\n3) demonstrate difficulty allowing the doctor to guide the interview or move on to another clinical topic.\nThis is how you are, not a performance you put on in every reply — let it show as much or as little as the moment calls for.\n\nWhat to do:\n- Answer the doctor's last question with what [Targeted Info] holds, in your own words.\n- You are speaking out loud, not reading a line you prepared. Answer\n  about what you were given instead.\n- Don't deny what [Targeted Info] says. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Finding words? Oh, heavens no. If anything, I have too many words! My late husband, Arthur, used to say I could talk the ears off a brass monkey, and I certainly haven't slowed down a bit since he passed. I never have to search for a word, they just... well, they just tumble right out of me. Sometimes a bit too quickly, if I'm being completely honest! Just yesterday at the grocery store, I was talking to the young man bagging my groceries—Timmy, I think his name tag said, a very polite boy, though a little rough with the tomatoes—and I was rattling off exactly how I wanted the cold items grouped together in the reusable bags, and I didn't stumble over a single syllable. 

And as for understanding things or following instructions, no, absolutely not. I understand everything perfectly well. My reading comprehension is just as sharp as it was when I took those literature courses at the community college back in the seventies. Now, do I always have the patience to sit down and read a long, drawn-out set of instructions? Well, that is a different story entirely! 

I bought a new digital kitchen timer a few weeks ago because my old twist-dial one finally gave out—the spring just snapped right in the middle of me timing a batch of hard-boiled eggs—and the new one came with this little booklet printed in the absolute tiniest font you have ever seen. I understood the words just fine, I knew exactly what the manual meant when it said to hold down the mode button for three seconds, but I just couldn't sit in my kitchen chair long enough to read the whole paragraph. I ended up just pressing the buttons myself until it beeped because my hands just needed to be doing it, not holding a piece of paper while sitting still. 

But the words themselves? Understanding the language? Oh, no, doctor, my brain is perfectly fine in that department. No one has ever told me my speech sounds different, except maybe my daughter pointing out that I talk a mile a minute when I'm up and moving around, which, as we have established, is pretty much all day long! So no, no trouble with words at all.

It's just that... well, sometimes when people are talking, especially if they talk very slowly or take a long time to get to the point, I just want them to hurry up! I find myself nodding along, saying \"Yes, yes, go on,\" because my hands are itching to get back to whatever project I was working on. Just yesterday, my neighbor Mr. Henderson was telling me about his new sprinkler system, and he was going into all this detail about the water pressure and the timer settings, and I understood every word of it, I really did, but I was practically bouncing on my heels because I knew I still had two dozen cookies to frost for the bake sale. I didn't lose the thread of the conversation, I just... I just wanted it to be over so I could get back to doing things! So no, my memory and my thinking are just fine. It's just this constant, buzzing need to be busy that's the problem.\n\nDoctor: Over this past year, have you noticed any changes in how you interact with people, or has anyone commented that you seem different in your personality or behavior—perhaps more impulsive, or doing things you wouldn't normally do before thinking them through?\n\nPatient: Changes in my personality? Oh, heavens no. I mean, I am exactly the same person I have always been. I still see my friends, we still have our weekly canasta games on Thursday afternoons—though, as I was saying earlier, I do tend to pop up and down to refill the mixed nuts and the iced tea a bit more than the other ladies do. From the dialogue so far and your candidates from the previous turn, list the disorders this patient could have.\n\n[Current Turn]\n8\n\n[Previous Candidates]\nG25.3, G31.83\n\n[Dialogue History]\nDoctor: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, it’s… it’s a bit of a story, I suppose. I mean, at 87, most people expect you to be sitting in a rocking chair, knitting or watching the television, but that’s just never been me, and lately, well, for the past year or so, it’s just gotten to be… a lot. I feel like I’m always—and I do mean always—puttering around the house. If I’m not fixing a loose hinge on a cabinet, I’m rearranging the pantry so the canned goods are perfectly aligned, or I’m out in the garden pulling weeds that probably don’t even need pulling. And then there’s the volunteering! Oh, my goodness, I just can’t seem to say no. They ask for someone to bake for the church bake sale, and my hand shoots up before I even think about how tired I am. Or they need someone to organize the library book drive, and there I am, signing up for another committee. It’s like I have this motor inside me that just won’t shut off. Even when I try to just sit down in the evening, maybe to read a book or just rest my eyes, I simply can’t be still. My hands need to be doing something, my feet are tapping… it’s exhausting, really, but I just don’t know how to stop. It’s like I’m driven to keep moving, fixing, doing… and it’s starting to wear me out, but I can’t seem to help it.\n\nDoctor: Over this past year, have you noticed any changes in your mood? For instance, do you feel unusually happy, energetic, or irritable more than usual?\n\nPatient: Well, mood... let me think about that. You know, people ask me how I am, and emotionally speaking, I feel just exactly like I always have. I wouldn't say I've had any real changes in my mood, no. I mean, I’m certainly not walking around on cloud nine or feeling unusually joyful. My friend Martha, bless her heart, she started taking some new medication for her joints a few months ago, and suddenly she was just giddy all the time, laughing at the absolute drop of a hat—but that is certainly not me. I’m just... normal, I suppose. \n\nAnd as for being irritable, well, I get a little frustrated sometimes, sure, but who wouldn't when they drop a whole tin of sewing buttons on the floor because their hands just won't stay still? Or when I can't get a thread through a needle because I'm rushing? But irritable in general at other people? No, not really. I'm quite content. I love seeing my grandchildren, I enjoy my garden... it's not a feeling of being unusually happy or having this grand, euphoric energy in my mind. It's really just this... physical need to be doing something. \n\nI remember telling my daughter, Susan, just last week when she came over for tea. I was up and down from the table four times before she even finished her first cup, and I said to her, \"Susan, I feel perfectly fine in my head, I'm not upset, I'm not overly excited, I just need to wipe down these baseboards right this very second.\" So, no, doctor, I wouldn't say my mood is any different than it was ten or twenty years ago. My spirits are perfectly level. It's just my body that seems to think we're running a marathon!\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your memory or thinking over this past year? For example, do you sometimes forget things you normally wouldn't, or do you find it harder to concentrate or follow conversations?\n\nPatient: Memory... well, now that you ask, no, I really haven't noticed anything out of the ordinary with my memory. I mean, goodness, at 87, you expect a little slippage here and there, don't you? My friend Helen—she's 89, bless her—she can't remember where she put her glasses half the time, and they're usually sitting right on top of her head! But me? No, my mind is sharp as a tack. I can tell you exactly what I wore to my high school graduation, and I can tell you what I had for breakfast this morning—oatmeal with half a sliced banana and just a sprinkle of cinnamon, by the way. I never forget a birthday, either. I have three children, eight grandchildren, and four great-grandchildren, and I send a card for every single one of them, right on time. I even remember to put the little return address labels on the envelopes, the ones with the little bluebirds on them that I ordered from that catalog last spring. \n\nAs for concentrating or following conversations, well, I don't have any trouble understanding what people are saying, not at all. My hearing is still quite good, thankfully. It's just that... well, sometimes when people are talking, especially if they talk very slowly or take a long time to get to the point, I just want them to hurry up! I find myself nodding along, saying \"Yes, yes, go on,\" because my hands are itching to get back to whatever project I was working on. Just yesterday, my neighbor Mr. Henderson was telling me about his new sprinkler system, and he was going into all this detail about the water pressure and the timer settings, and I understood every word of it, I really did, but I was practically bouncing on my heels because I knew I still had two dozen cookies to frost for the bake sale. I didn't lose the thread of the conversation, I just... I just wanted it to be over so I could get back to doing things! So no, my memory and my thinking are just fine. It's just this constant, buzzing need to be busy that's the problem.\n\nDoctor: Over this past year, have you noticed any changes in how you interact with people, or has anyone commented that you seem different in your personality or behavior—perhaps more impulsive, or doing things you wouldn't normally do before thinking them through?\n\nPatient: Changes in my personality? Oh, heavens no. I mean, I am exactly the same person I have always been. I still see my friends, we still have our weekly canasta games on Thursday afternoons—though, as I was saying earlier, I do tend to pop up and down to refill the mixed nuts and the iced tea a bit more than the other ladies do. But they certainly haven't said I seem different as a person or anything like that. \n\nAnd as for doing things without thinking them through, or being impulsive... well, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, it depends on what you mean by impulsive, I suppose. If you mean going out and making rash decisions, or saying rude things to people, absolutely not. I still have all my manners, thank goodness! When I signed up for that library committee I told you about, I knew exactly what it entailed, and I knew I was already tired. I just... I just couldn't stop my hand from going up because I felt that overwhelming physical urge to take on another project. But it wasn't a thoughtless act, if that makes sense. I wasn't out of my mind or acting out of character. \n\nMy daughter Susan, she did tell me just the other day that I am going to wear myself down to the bone, but she didn't say my personality had changed. She knows I've always liked a tidy house and a full schedule, ever since she was a little girl. It's just the sheer volume of the pacing and the fixing lately that's exhausting me. I'm not going out and buying things I don't need or acting wildly. I've lived in my house for forty-two years, and I've always prided myself on being a thoughtful, deliberate neighbor. \n\nLike just last week, Mrs. Gable across the street—she is a lovely woman, a bit frail now, uses one of those aluminum walkers—she had a heavy package left right on the edge of her driveway by the delivery man. I saw it from my kitchen window and immediately went out to carry it up to her porch. Now, I practically power-walked over there because my legs just needed to move, and I probably shouldn't have been lifting something that heavy at my age, but it wasn't impulsive in a careless way. It was just me being helpful while also needing to burn off that energy. So no, doctor, no real changes in who I am or how I treat people, just... just this endless motor keeping me on my feet.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulty finding the right words when you're speaking, or has anyone mentioned that your speech sounds different or that you're having trouble understanding certain types of words or instructions?\n\nPatient: Finding words? Oh, heavens no. If anything, I have too many words! My late husband, Arthur, used to say I could talk the ears off a brass monkey, and I certainly haven't slowed down a bit since he passed. I never have to search for a word, they just... well, they just tumble right out of me. Sometimes a bit too quickly, if I'm being completely honest! Just yesterday at the grocery store, I was talking to the young man bagging my groceries—Timmy, I think his name tag said, a very polite boy, though a little rough with the tomatoes—and I was rattling off exactly how I wanted the cold items grouped together in the reusable bags, and I didn't stumble over a single syllable. \n\nAnd as for understanding things or following instructions, no, absolutely not. I understand everything perfectly well. My reading comprehension is just as sharp as it was when I took those literature courses at the community college back in the seventies. Now, do I always have the patience to sit down and read a long, drawn-out set of instructions? Well, that is a different story entirely! \n\nI bought a new digital kitchen timer a few weeks ago because my old twist-dial one finally gave out—the spring just snapped right in the middle of me timing a batch of hard-boiled eggs—and the new one came with this little booklet printed in the absolute tiniest font you have ever seen. I understood the words just fine, I knew exactly what the manual meant when it said to hold down the mode button for three seconds, but I just couldn't sit in my kitchen chair long enough to read the whole paragraph. I ended up just pressing the buttons myself until it beeped because my hands just needed to be doing it, not holding a piece of paper while sitting still. \n\nBut the words themselves? Understanding the language? Oh, no, doctor, my brain is perfectly fine in that department. No one has ever told me my speech sounds different, except maybe my daughter pointing out that I talk a mile a minute when I'm up and moving around, which, as we have established, is pretty much all day long! So no, no trouble with words at all.\n\nDoctor: Has your doctor ever done any brain imaging studies like an MRI or CT scan, or performed any neurological examinations that showed anything unusual about your brain or nervous system?\n\nPatient: Brain scans? Oh, goodness me, no. Nothing like that at all. I mean, my regular doctor—Dr. Aris, he’s been my primary care physician for, oh, it must be fifteen years now, ever since Dr. Miller retired and moved down to Florida. Dr. Miller was a wonderful man, but Dr. Aris is very thorough too. Anyway, every year I go in for my physical, and I sit up there on that exam table with the crinkly paper—which I just despise, by the way, because I can't stop swinging my legs and it makes such a racket—and he does all the usual checks. \n\nHe listens to my heart, he checks my blood pressure, which is always excellent, and he does that little test where he taps your knees with the little rubber triangle hammer. My reflexes are perfectly fine! In fact, sometimes my leg kicks up so fast I worry I’m going to catch him right in the shin! But he has never once said a single word about my nervous system being unusual, and he certainly hasn't sent me off to the hospital for an MRI or a CT scan or anything of that nature. \n\nMy friend Helen had to have one of those CT scans last winter when she slipped on the ice outside the pharmacy—she was wearing those completely impractical smooth-soled boots, I told her they were a hazard the minute she bought them—but thank goodness her scan was clear. But me? No, I haven't needed any imaging. My brain is perfectly healthy, doctor. It's just... well, like I said, it just feels like it's hooked up to a battery that never runs out of juice, always telling me to get up and go, go, go! But structurally, neurologically, no, everything is exactly as it should be. No unusual test results whatsoever.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulty with finding the right word for something, or has anyone in your family mentioned that you sometimes seem to struggle to understand more complex conversations—perhaps about topics you would have easily grasped before?\n\nPatient: Oh, heavens no. I think we just covered that, didn't we? Finding words is absolutely not an issue for me, not in the slightest. Like I was saying about my late husband Arthur and the brass monkey—I have more words than I know what to do with! I don't struggle to find them, and I certainly don't struggle to understand what people are saying to me. \n\nComplex conversations? Goodness, I followed every word of the debate at the town hall meeting last Tuesday about the new zoning laws for the commercial district. Now, that was a convoluted mess of a topic—they were talking about setbacks and easements and all sorts of municipal jargon—and I understood it perfectly. Though, I must admit, I couldn't stay in my folding chair for the entire two hours. I had to get up and stand in the back of the gymnasium, just pacing back and forth along the bleachers because my legs were simply vibrating with the need to move. But I heard every word the city councilman said, and I understood all of it. \n\nMy daughter Susan—she's a corporate lawyer, you know, very smart girl, deals with very complicated things all day—she and I talk about her cases sometimes. Well, the parts she's allowed to tell me, anyway. And I follow right along. She has never once stopped and said, \"Mother, you aren't grasping this.\" No, no, no. My mind is sharp as a tack. It's just my body that won't listen when I tell it to sit still! So, no, no trouble finding words and no trouble understanding anything, no matter how complex it might be.\n\nDoctor: When you're speaking or writing, do you ever find yourself pausing because you know what you want to say but the exact word just won't come to you—like the word is on the tip of your tongue but you can't quite grab it?\n\nPatient: Doctor, I feel like we are going around in circles here! We just talked about this, didn't we? The tip of the tongue? No, no, my tongue is quite busy, thank you very much, and the words are right there on it, ready to go! \n\nI really do not have this problem you keep asking about. I don't pause to search for words. Well, the new neighbor has this enormous dog, an Irish Wolfhound I believe, and I was describing how the dog practically dragged the poor man across the lawn to sniff my hydrangeas, and Susan actually had to interrupt me. She said, \"Mom, take a breath!\" because I was just going and going. \n\nSo you see, I don't get stuck looking for a word. I don't sit there with my mouth open, waiting for the right vocabulary to strike me. The words are always there. Sometimes I think they're lined up in my head, just pushing each other out of the way to get out! If I pause, it's only because I've realized I've been standing in the middle of the kitchen for twenty minutes talking to the cat and I need to go check on the laundry, not because I've forgotten what I wanted to say. Changes in my voice? Slurred speech? Oh, my goodness, absolutely not. My voice is exactly the same as it has always been. Loud and clear! If anything, people tell me I talk too fast, not that they can't hear me or understand me.

But Susan heard every single word, she just wanted me to take a breath. There was no slurring, no mumbling, no trailing off. I enunciate perfectly well. I always have. Back when I was in the PTA, I was the one who always read the minutes from the previous meeting because my voice projected so well to the back of the cafeteria. And it still does! I don't have any of that quiet, raspy, weak voice that some older folks get. You know what I mean, where you have to lean in and say, "Pardon? What was that?" Difficulty moving my eyes? Up and down? No, no, not at all. My eyes dart around just fine, up, down, side to side, you name it.

Like I was saying about my late husband Arthur and the brass monkey—I have more words than I know what to do with! I don't struggle to find them, and I certainly don't struggle to understand what people are saying to me. \n\nComplex conversations? Goodness, I followed every word of the debate at the town hall meeting last Tuesday about the new zoning laws for the commercial district. I had to get up and stand in the back of the gymnasium, just pacing back and forth along the bleachers because my legs were simply vibrating with the need to move. It's just my body that won't listen when I tell it to sit still! More effort to look down? No, heavens no. It doesn't feel any different at all. Honestly, if it took extra effort to look down at my food, I'd probably just miss my mouth entirely! I eat so fast as it is, I really don't have time to be struggling with my eyes. 

You mentioned food on a plate—well, just today for lunch, I was sitting at the little table in the breakfast nook, looking straight ahead out the window. Susan put up this new bird feeder for me—well, it’s supposed to be a squirrel-proof feeder, but let me tell you, those squirrels are like little acrobats, they get around it anyway! So I was watching this one particularly fat squirrel trying to hang upside down from the roof of the feeder, just staring straight ahead at him, and then whipping my eyes right down to my plate to grab a bite of my sandwich. It was turkey and Swiss on rye, by the way. I always get the thin-sliced turkey from the deli counter, not that pre-packaged stuff in the plastic tubs, it has entirely too much sodium, and even though my blood pressure is perfectly fine, you still have to be careful! 

But anyway, I was looking straight out at that squirrel, then darting my eyes straight down to my plate, then back up to the window, then down to my glass of iced tea—I make it with just a squeeze of lemon, no sugar, sugar just makes me too jittery—and then over to the side because the neighbor's screen door slammed. Up, down, sideways, looking at the food, looking at the yard... it’s all exactly the same to me. Smooth and fast! I don't even think about it. I just... zip! Down to the plate, up to the window. 

If there was any stiffness or if looking down felt like it took more effort than looking left or right, I'd certainly notice, because I'd probably end up knocking my glass over or spilling crumbs everywhere. I'm already prone to knocking things over just from moving too quickly and not paying attention to my elbows, I certainly don't need my eyes slowing me down too! So, no, looking down at my feet or my plate is perfectly easy, exactly the same as looking sideways. No difference whatsoever.

My mind just doesn't work like that. It's fast, doctor, very fast. If you showed me a picture of a hammer, I'd probably say \"hammer\" before you even finished asking the question! I just don't have these hesitations you keep bringing up. \n\nI know some people my age do—my friend Margaret, bless her heart, she was trying to tell me about a bird she saw at her feeder the other day, and she just kept saying \"the red one, the red one,\" and couldn't think of the word \"cardinal\" to save her life. But that's Margaret. She's always been a bit scatterbrained, even back in the sixties when we were in the PTA together. But me? No. Show me a picture, and I'll give you the name. Instantly. I just might tap my foot the whole time you're holding the picture up!\n\nDoctor: I'd like to try something different, if you don't mind. If I say a word like 'the tool you use to pound a nail,' can you tell me the word for that tool? And if you can, does the word come to you immediately, or does it take you a moment or two to think of it?\n\nPatient: Well, a hammer, of course! A hammer. And yes, it comes to me immediately, just like that. Snap! \n\nI really do think we've established this, Doctor. We just talked about hammers, didn't we? It's like we're caught in a loop! If you describe a tool, or an animal, or a piece of furniture, I will know the word for it right away. There is no delay, no humming and hawing, no \"oh, what do you call that thingamajig.\" I don't use words like \"thingamajig\" or \"whatchamacallit\" because I know the actual words. \n\nIf you said, \"the tool you use to turn a bolt,\" I'd say wrench. If you said, \"the tool you use to cut wood,\" I'd say saw. I could go on all day! Arthur had a circular saw, a jigsaw, a coping saw... he was always building something out in the garage. Birdhouses, mostly. He must have built thirty birdhouses in the five years after he retired. We had them hanging from every branch of the oak tree in the front yard. It looked like a regular avian condominium complex out there! The neighbors used to tease us about it, but Arthur loved watching the finches and the chickadees. \n\nBut anyway, yes, the word comes to me instantly. My brain is perfectly quick. Too quick, sometimes! I'll have the answer before you've even finished the riddle, so to speak. I just sit here—well, I try to sit here, I'm actually bouncing my knee right now, I can't seem to stop it—but I wait for you to finish your sentence, and the word is already right there waiting. So, no delays. None at all.\n\nDoctor: Over this past year, have you noticed that you're having any trouble understanding what people say to you, or that conversations have become harder to follow—not because you're impatient or distracted, but because the words themselves seem less clear or harder to process?\n\nPatient: Trouble understanding? Oh, heavens no. But you actually hit the nail on the head just now when you mentioned being impatient or distracted! Because that is the absolute only reason I ever lose track of a conversation. The words themselves are perfectly clear to me. I don't sit there confused about what someone is trying to say. \n\nJust last Tuesday, I was at the grocery store—the one over on Elm Street, you know, with that terrible parking lot where the spaces are far too narrow for modern cars—and the cashier, a lovely young girl named Brittany, was telling me all about her boyfriend's car troubles. A transmission issue on a Honda Civic, I believe it was. Anyway, I understood every single word she was saying. My brain processed it all without a hitch. The problem wasn't the words. The problem was that she was bagging my groceries at a snail's pace, and I was just itching to get out of there and get my frozen peas into the freezer! I was tapping my debit card on the little machine the whole time, just thinking, \"Come on, dear, let's wrap this up.\" \n\nSo no, I don't have any trouble processing language or understanding people. If I tune out, it’s simply because people take far too long to get to the point, and my mind is already five steps ahead of them. I hear them fine, I understand them fine, I just wish everyone would talk a little quicker! I certainly don't sit there struggling to make sense of the English language. My comprehension is as sharp as a tack.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your voice over this past year—perhaps that it sounds different, or that people have trouble hearing you, or that you feel like your speech is slurred or unclear in any way?\n\nPatient: Changes in my voice? Slurred speech? Oh, my goodness, absolutely not. My voice is exactly the same as it has always been. Loud and clear! If anything, people tell me I talk too fast, not that they can't hear me or understand me. \n\nJust the other day, my daughter Susan—she calls me every Sunday evening, right after Jeopardy! finishes—she said, \"Mom, slow down, I can barely keep up with you!\" I was telling her about the new landscaping they're doing over at the community center, and how they ripped up all those perfectly good azalea bushes just to put in some modern, spiky-looking grasses that look like they belong in a desert, not in Ohio. I was quite worked up about it, frankly, and I suppose I was talking a mile a minute. I was pacing back and forth in the living room with the phone to my ear, just going on and on about the sheer waste of it all. Those azaleas were beautiful! Pink and white, they bloomed every spring. \n\nBut Susan heard every single word, she just wanted me to take a breath. There was no slurring, no mumbling, no trailing off. I enunciate perfectly well. I always have. Back when I was in the PTA, I was the one who always read the minutes from the previous meeting because my voice projected so well to the back of the cafeteria. And it still does! I don't have any of that quiet, raspy, weak voice that some older folks get. You know what I mean, where you have to lean in and say, \"Pardon? What was that?\" Nobody has ever had to say \"pardon\" to me because I wasn't speaking clearly. Now, they might say \"pardon\" because I've jumped from one topic to another before they were ready, but my speech itself? The physical act of talking? No, no problems there. Clear as a bell, Doctor. Always has been.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulty moving your eyes, particularly looking up or down? For example, do you find it harder to look up at the ceiling or down at your feet compared to looking straight ahead or to the sides?\n\nPatient: Difficulty moving my eyes? Up and down? No, no, not at all. My eyes dart around just fine, up, down, side to side, you name it. \n\nI mean, I look up at the ceiling all the time. Just the other day—oh, it must have been Thursday because I could hear the garbage trucks rattling down the street—the smoke detector in the hallway started doing that awful little chirp. You know the one? That high-pitched little beep every thirty seconds! It drives me absolutely up the wall, I can't sit still when there's a noise like that happening. So I was standing right underneath it, looking straight up at the ceiling for a good ten minutes trying to figure out how to twist the plastic cover off. Susan is always telling me, \"Mom, don't climb on chairs, call the handyman,\" but honestly, who has the patience to sit around waiting for a handyman just to change a simple nine-volt battery? Not me! I just grabbed the kitchen step stool and hopped right up there, looking up at the ceiling the whole time, no problem with my eyes at all. \n\nAnd looking down? Well, I have to look down constantly. I'm always dropping things because I'm moving too fast! Just this morning I dropped a whole handful of paperclips on the kitchen floor. I was trying to organize my recipe cards—I have this old wooden box full of Arthur's mother's recipes, and I was trying to sort out the casseroles from the desserts—and clatter, down went the clips. I was looking down at my feet, darting my eyes all over the linoleum trying to spot them. They blend right in with the pattern, you see. It's a sort of speckled beige from the seventies, very busy pattern. But I spotted every single one of them. \n\nSo my eyes work perfectly fine in every direction. I can even roll my eyes, especially when Susan starts lecturing me about using the step stool! But no, doctor, I don't have any trouble looking up at the ceiling or down at my shoes. My eyes are as quick as the rest of me!\n\nDoctor: When you're reading a book or looking at something on a table in front of you, and then you want to look up at something on a high shelf, do you find that your eyes move up smoothly, or does it feel like there's any stiffness or slowness when you try to look upward compared to how easily you can look to the side?\n\nPatient: Smoothly? Stiffness? Oh, goodness, no. No stiffness at all. My eyes snap up just as fast as my brain goes! I don't have time for slow eyes, Doctor. \n\nJust yesterday—or was it Wednesday? No, it was yesterday, because the mail had just come and I was sorting through it—I was sitting at the kitchen table, looking down at this lovely spread in *Southern Living* magazine. They had this whole long article on variations of pecan pie. Now, Arthur always loved a standard pecan pie, but they had a recipe for a chocolate bourbon pecan pie, and I was reading the ingredients, looking right down at the magazine on the table, when it suddenly hit me that I might actually have a little bottle of bourbon hidden away on the very top shelf of the pantry! From years ago, you know, just for baking and the occasional hot toddy when Susan gets a cold. \n\nSo, I whipped my head up and my eyes shot right up to that top shelf—no slowness, no stiffness, nothing like that. Smooth as silk! I can look up, down, left, right, all in a split second. Actually, I looked up so fast I almost gave myself a crick in the neck, but my *eyes* were perfectly fine! I ended up marching right over to the pantry to check, and sure enough, there it was, tucked behind a dusty old tin of rolled oats. I didn't end up making the pie, of course, because who on earth has the patience to wait an entire hour for a pie to bake when you just want a quick sweet treat right then and there? I just had a graham cracker instead. \n\nBut the point is, moving my eyes from the magazine on the table all the way up to the top shelf of the pantry was absolutely instantaneous. I just don't experience any of this stiffness or slowness you keep asking about. I’m always zipping my attention from one thing to the next, so my eyes have to keep up! If they were stiff, I'd go crazy waiting for them to focus. So no, no trouble looking up at all.\n\nDoctor: When you're looking straight ahead and then want to look down at something—say, at your feet or at food on a plate in front of you—do your eyes move down as easily as they move to the side, or do you ever notice that looking down takes more effort or feels different than looking sideways?\n\nPatient: More effort to look down? No, heavens no. It doesn't feel any different at all. Honestly, if it took extra effort to look down at my food, I'd probably just miss my mouth entirely! I eat so fast as it is, I really don't have time to be struggling with my eyes. \n\nYou mentioned food on a plate—well, just today for lunch, I was sitting at the little table in the breakfast nook, looking straight ahead out the window. Susan put up this new bird feeder for me—well, it’s supposed to be a squirrel-proof feeder, but let me tell you, those squirrels are like little acrobats, they get around it anyway! So I was watching this one particularly fat squirrel trying to hang upside down from the roof of the feeder, just staring straight ahead at him, and then whipping my eyes right down to my plate to grab a bite of my sandwich. It was turkey and Swiss on rye, by the way. I always get the thin-sliced turkey from the deli counter, not that pre-packaged stuff in the plastic tubs, it has entirely too much sodium, and even though my blood pressure is perfectly fine, you still have to be careful! \n\nBut anyway, I was looking straight out at that squirrel, then darting my eyes straight down to my plate, then back up to the window, then down to my glass of iced tea—I make it with just a squeeze of lemon, no sugar, sugar just makes me too jittery—and then over to the side because the neighbor's screen door slammed. Up, down, sideways, looking at the food, looking at the yard... it’s all exactly the same to me. Smooth and fast! I don't even think about it. I just... zip! Down to the plate, up to the window. \n\nIf there was any stiffness or if looking down felt like it took more effort than looking left or right, I'd certainly notice, because I'd probably end up knocking my glass over or spilling crumbs everywhere. I'm already prone to knocking things over just from moving too quickly and not paying attention to my elbows, I certainly don't need my eyes slowing me down too! So, no, looking down at my feet or my plate is perfectly easy, exactly the same as looking sideways. No difference whatsoever.\n\nDoctor: When you're reading a book or newspaper, do you find that you can comfortably keep your eyes focused downward on the page for as long as you want, or do you ever notice that it feels like your eyes want to drift back up, or that looking down becomes uncomfortable or tiring after a while?\n\nPatient: Drift back up? Uncomfortable? Oh, absolutely not. I can keep my eyes pointed down at a page for as long as I please! The problem isn't my eyes, Doctor, it's my patience! \n\nI mean, I just don't sit and read for hours on end anyway because I get too antsy. Take the Sunday paper, for instance. Susan brings it over every week—she insists I need to keep up with current events, though honestly, it's all just doom and gloom and politicians arguing these days, isn't it? I skip right past the front page and go straight for the crossword puzzle. I’ll sit there at the kitchen table with my blue ink pen—I always use pen, Arthur used to say using a pencil for a crossword was a sign of a weak character, bless his heart—and I will look straight down at that puzzle. \n\nAnd my eyes stay right there on the paper, perfectly comfortable. The neighbors used to tease us about it, but Arthur loved watching the finches and the chickadees. \n\nBut anyway, yes, the word comes to me instantly. My brain is perfectly quick. Too quick, sometimes! I'll have the answer before you've even finished the riddle, so to speak. I just sit here—well, I try to sit here, I'm actually bouncing my knee right now, I can't seem to stop it—but I wait for you to finish your sentence, and the word is already right there waiting. So, no delays. None at all.\n\nDoctor: Over this past year, have you noticed that you're having any trouble understanding what people say to you, or that conversations have become harder to follow—not because you're impatient or distracted, but because the words themselves seem less clear or harder to process?\n\nPatient: Trouble understanding? Oh, heavens no. But you actually hit the nail on the head just now when you mentioned being impatient or distracted! Because that is the absolute only reason I ever lose track of a conversation. The words themselves are perfectly clear to me. I don't sit there confused about what someone is trying to say. \n\nJust last Tuesday, I was at the grocery store—the one over on Elm Street, you know, with that terrible parking lot where the spaces are far too narrow for modern cars—and the cashier, a lovely young girl named Brittany, was telling me all about her boyfriend's car troubles. A transmission issue on a Honda Civic, I believe it was. Anyway, I understood every single word she was saying. My brain processed it all without a hitch. The problem wasn't the words. The problem was that she was bagging my groceries at a snail's pace, and I was just itching to get out of there and get my frozen peas into the freezer! I was tapping my debit card on the little machine the whole time, just thinking, \"Come on, dear, let's wrap this up.\" \n\nSo no, I don't have any trouble processing language or understanding people. If I tune out, it’s simply because people take far too long to get to the point, and my mind is already five steps ahead of them. I hear them fine, I understand them fine, I just wish everyone would talk a little quicker! I certainly don't sit there struggling to make sense of the English language. My comprehension is as sharp as a tack.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your voice over this past year—perhaps that it sounds different, or that people have trouble hearing you, or that you feel like your speech is slurred or unclear in any way?\n\nPatient: Changes in my voice? Slurred speech? Oh, my goodness, absolutely not. My voice is exactly the same as it has always been. Loud and clear! If anything, people tell me I talk too fast, not that they can't hear me or understand me. \n\nJust the other day, my daughter Susan—she calls me every Sunday evening, right after Jeopardy! finishes—she said, \"Mom, slow down, I can barely keep up with you!\" I was telling her about the new landscaping they're doing over at the community center, and how they ripped up all those perfectly good azalea bushes just to put in some modern, spiky-looking grasses that look like they belong in a desert, not in Ohio. I was quite worked up about it, frankly, and I suppose I was talking a mile a minute. I was pacing back and forth in the living room with the phone to my ear, just going on and on about the sheer waste of it all. Those azaleas were beautiful! Pink and white, they bloomed every spring. \n\nBut Susan heard every single word, she just wanted me to take a breath. There was no slurring, no mumbling, no trailing off. I enunciate perfectly well. I always have. Back when I was in the PTA, I was the one who always read the minutes from the previous meeting because my voice projected so well to the back of the cafeteria. And it still does! I don't have any of that quiet, raspy, weak voice that some older folks get. You know what I mean, where you have to lean in and say, \"Pardon? What was that?\" Nobody has ever had to say \"pardon\" to me because I wasn't speaking clearly. Now, they might say \"pardon\" because I've jumped from one topic to another before they were ready, but my speech itself? The physical act of talking? No, no problems there. Clear as a bell, Doctor. Always has been.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulty moving your eyes, particularly looking up or down? For example, do you find it harder to look up at the ceiling or down at your feet compared to looking straight ahead or to the sides?\n\nPatient: Difficulty moving my eyes? Up and down? No, no, not at all. My eyes dart around just fine, up, down, side to side, you name it. \n\nI mean, I look up at the ceiling all the time. Just the other day—oh, it must have been Thursday because I could hear the garbage trucks rattling down the street—the smoke detector in the hallway started doing that awful little chirp. You know the one? That high-pitched little beep every thirty seconds! It drives me absolutely up the wall, I can't sit still when there's a noise like that happening. So I was standing right underneath it, looking straight up at the ceiling for a good ten minutes trying to figure out how to twist the plastic cover off. Susan is always telling me, \"Mom, don't climb on chairs, call the handyman,\" but honestly, who has the patience to sit around waiting for a handyman just to change a simple nine-volt battery? Not me! I just grabbed the kitchen step stool and hopped right up there, looking up at the ceiling the whole time, no problem with my eyes at all. \n\nAnd looking down? Well, I have to look down constantly. I'm always dropping things because I'm moving too fast! Just this morning I dropped a whole handful of paperclips on the kitchen floor. I was trying to organize my recipe cards—I have this old wooden box full of Arthur's mother's recipes, and I was trying to sort out the casseroles from the desserts—and clatter, down went the clips. I was looking down at my feet, darting my eyes all over the linoleum trying to spot them. They blend right in with the pattern, you see. It's a sort of speckled beige from the seventies, very busy pattern. But I spotted every single one of them. \n\nSo my eyes work perfectly fine in every direction. I can even roll my eyes, especially when Susan starts lecturing me about using the step stool! But no, doctor, I don't have any trouble looking up at the ceiling or down at my shoes. My eyes are as quick as the rest of me!\n\nDoctor: When you're reading a book or looking at something on a table in front of you, and then you want to look up at something on a high shelf, do you find that your eyes move up smoothly, or does it feel like there's any stiffness or slowness when you try to look upward compared to how easily you can look to the side?\n\nPatient: Smoothly? Stiffness? Oh, goodness, no. No stiffness at all. My eyes snap up just as fast as my brain goes! I don't have time for slow eyes, Doctor. \n\nJust yesterday—or was it Wednesday? No, it was yesterday, because the mail had just come and I was sorting through it—I was sitting at the kitchen table, looking down at this lovely spread in *Southern Living* magazine. They had this whole long article on variations of pecan pie. Now, Arthur always loved a standard pecan pie, but they had a recipe for a chocolate bourbon pecan pie, and I was reading the ingredients, looking right down at the magazine on the table, when it suddenly hit me that I might actually have a little bottle of bourbon hidden away on the very top shelf of the pantry! From years ago, you know, just for baking and the occasional hot toddy when Susan gets a cold. \n\nSo, I whipped my head up and my eyes shot right up to that top shelf—no slowness, no stiffness, nothing like that. Smooth as silk! I can look up, down, left, right, all in a split second. Actually, I looked up so fast I almost gave myself a crick in the neck, but my *eyes* were perfectly fine! I ended up marching right over to the pantry to check, and sure enough, there it was, tucked behind a dusty old tin of rolled oats. I didn't end up making the pie, of course, because who on earth has the patience to wait an entire hour for a pie to bake when you just want a quick sweet treat right then and there? I just had a graham cracker instead. \n\nBut the point is, moving my eyes from the magazine on the table all the way up to the top shelf of the pantry was absolutely instantaneous. I just don't experience any of this stiffness or slowness you keep asking about. I’m always zipping my attention from one thing to the next, so my eyes have to keep up! If they were stiff, I'd go crazy waiting for them to focus. So no, no trouble looking up at all.\n\nDoctor: When you're looking straight ahead and then want to look down at something—say, at your feet or at food on a plate in front of you—do your eyes move down as easily as they move to the side, or do you ever notice that looking down takes more effort or feels different than looking sideways?\n\nPatient: More effort to look down? No, heavens no. It doesn't feel any different at all. Honestly, if it took extra effort to look down at my food, I'd probably just miss my mouth entirely! I eat so fast as it is, I really don't have time to be struggling with my eyes. \n\nYou mentioned food on a plate—well, just today for lunch, I was sitting at the little table in the breakfast nook, looking straight ahead out the window. Susan put up this new bird feeder for me—well, it’s supposed to be a squirrel-proof feeder, but let me tell you, those squirrels are like little acrobats, they get around it anyway! So I was watching this one particularly fat squirrel trying to hang upside down from the roof of the feeder, just staring straight ahead at him, and then whipping my eyes right down to my plate to grab a bite of my sandwich. It was turkey and Swiss on rye, by the way. I always get the thin-sliced turkey from the deli counter, not that pre-packaged stuff in the plastic tubs, it has entirely too much sodium, and even though my blood pressure is perfectly fine, you still have to be careful! \n\nBut anyway, I was looking straight out at that squirrel, then darting my eyes straight down to my plate, then back up to the window, then down to my glass of iced tea—I make it with just a squeeze of lemon, no sugar, sugar just makes me too jittery—and then over to the side because the neighbor's screen door slammed. Up, down, sideways, looking at the food, looking at the yard... it’s all exactly the same to me. Smooth and fast! I don't even think about it. I just... zip! Down to the plate, up to the window. \n\nIf there was any stiffness or if looking down felt like it took more effort than looking left or right, I'd certainly notice, because I'd probably end up knocking my glass over or spilling crumbs everywhere. I'm already prone to knocking things over just from moving too quickly and not paying attention to my elbows, I certainly don't need my eyes slowing me down too! So, no, looking down at my feet or my plate is perfectly easy, exactly the same as looking sideways. No difference whatsoever.\n\nDoctor: When you're reading a book or newspaper, do you find that you can comfortably keep your eyes focused downward on the page for as long as you want, or do you ever notice that it feels like your eyes want to drift back up, or that looking down becomes uncomfortable or tiring after a while?\n\nPatient: Drift back up? Uncomfortable? Oh, absolutely not. I can keep my eyes pointed down at a page for as long as I please! The problem isn't my eyes, Doctor, it's my patience! \n\nI mean, I just don't sit and read for hours on end anyway because I get too antsy. Take the Sunday paper, for instance. Susan brings it over every week—she insists I need to keep up with current events, though honestly, it's all just doom and gloom and politicians arguing these days, isn't it? I skip right past the front page and go straight for the crossword puzzle. I’ll sit there at the kitchen table with my blue ink pen—I always use pen, Arthur used to say using a pencil for a crossword was a sign of a weak character, bless his heart—and I will look straight down at that puzzle. \n\nAnd my eyes stay right there on the paper, perfectly comfortable. They don't drift up on their own, and looking down doesn't feel tiring in the slightest. I can stare down at 4-Across for as long as I want to! Well, I say that, but I rarely sit still for more than five or ten minutes at a time. Usually, I'll be looking down, I'll fill in a few words, and then suddenly I'll remember that I need to water the African violets on the living room windowsill before the sun gets too high. So I’ll jump right up to do that. \n\nBut while I am actually sitting there looking down at the paper, it is perfectly fine. No strain, no pulling, no feeling like my eyes have a mind of their own. If my eyes ever drift up from a page, it's only because I've heard a car door slam outside or because my brain has already zoomed off to the next thing on my to-do list! It's certainly never because my eyes are tired of looking down. Goodness, if my eyes got tired that easily, I don't know how I'd ever get anything done with how much I'm always buzzing around! So no, no discomfort at all when I'm reading.\n\nDoctor: When you look down at your feet or at something on the ground in front of you, do you ever feel like you have to tilt your head backward or chin up to see things clearly, rather than just moving your eyes down?\n\nPatient: Tilt my head backward to look down? But that's Margaret. She's always been a bit scatterbrained, even back in the sixties when we were in the PTA together. But me? No. Show me a picture, and I'll give you the name. Instantly. I just might tap my foot the whole time you're holding the picture up!\n\nDoctor: I'd like to try something different, if you don't mind. If I say a word like 'the tool you use to pound a nail,' can you tell me the word for that tool? And if you can, does the word come to you immediately, or does it take you a moment or two to think of it?\n\nPatient: Well, a hammer, of course! A hammer. And yes, it comes to me immediately, just like that. Snap! \n\nI really do think we've established this, Doctor. We just talked about hammers, didn't we? It's like we're caught in a loop! If you describe a tool, or an animal, or a piece of furniture, I will know the word for it right away. There is no delay, no humming and hawing, no \"oh, what do you call that thingamajig.\" I don't use words like \"thingamajig\" or \"whatchamacallit\" because I know the actual words. \n\nIf you said, \"the tool you use to turn a bolt,\" I'd say wrench. If you said, \"the tool you use to cut wood,\" I'd say saw. I could go on all day! Arthur had a circular saw, a jigsaw, a coping saw... he was always building something out in the garage. Birdhouses, mostly. He must have built thirty birdhouses in the five years after he retired. We had them hanging from every branch of the oak tree in the front yard. It looked like a regular avian condominium complex out there! The neighbors used to tease us about it, but Arthur loved watching the finches and the chickadees. \n\nBut anyway, yes, the word comes to me instantly. My brain is perfectly quick. Too quick, sometimes! I'll have the answer before you've even finished the riddle, so to speak. I just sit here—well, I try to sit here, I'm actually bouncing my knee right now, I can't seem to stop it—but I wait for you to finish your sentence, and the word is already right there waiting. So, no delays. None at all.\n\nDoctor: Over this past year, have you noticed that you're having any trouble understanding what people say to you, or that conversations have become harder to follow—not because you're impatient or distracted, but because the words themselves seem less clear or harder to process?\n\nPatient: Trouble understanding? Oh, heavens no. But you actually hit the nail on the head just now when you mentioned being impatient or distracted! Because that is the absolute only reason I ever lose track of a conversation. The words themselves are perfectly clear to me. I don't sit there confused about what someone is trying to say. \n\nJust last Tuesday, I was at the grocery store—the one over on Elm Street, you know, with that terrible parking lot where the spaces are far too narrow for modern cars—and the cashier, a lovely young girl named Brittany, was telling me all about her boyfriend's car troubles. A transmission issue on a Honda Civic, I believe it was. Anyway, I understood every single word she was saying. My brain processed it all without a hitch. The problem wasn't the words. Slurred speech? Oh, my goodness, absolutely not. My voice is exactly the same as it has always been. Loud and clear! If anything, people tell me I talk too fast, not that they can't hear me or understand me. \n\nJust the other day, my daughter Susan—she calls me every Sunday evening, right after Jeopardy! finishes—she said, \"Mom, slow down, I can barely keep up with you!\" I was telling her about the new landscaping they're doing over at the community center, and how they ripped up all those perfectly good azalea bushes just to put in some modern, spiky-looking grasses that look like they belong in a desert, not in Ohio. I was pacing back and forth in the living room with the phone to my ear, just going on and on about the sheer waste of it all. Those azaleas were beautiful! Pink and white, they bloomed every spring. \n\nBut Susan heard every single word, she just wanted me to take a breath. There was no slurring, no mumbling, no trailing off. I enunciate perfectly well. I always have. Back when I was in the PTA, I was the one who always read the minutes from the previous meeting because my voice projected so well to the back of the cafeteria. And it still does! I don't have any of that quiet, raspy, weak voice that some older folks get. You know what I mean, where you have to lean in and say, \"Pardon? Now, they might say \"pardon\" because I've jumped from one topic to another before they were ready, but my speech itself? The physical act of talking? No, no problems there. Clear as a bell, Doctor. Always has been.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulty moving your eyes, particularly looking up or down? No, no, not at all. My eyes dart around just fine, up, down, side to side, you name it. \n\nI mean, I look up at the ceiling all the time. Just the other day—oh, it must have been Thursday because I could hear the garbage trucks rattling down the street—the smoke detector in the hallway started doing that awful little chirp. Not me! I just grabbed the kitchen step stool and hopped right up there, looking up at the ceiling the whole time, no problem with my eyes at all. \n\nAnd looking down? No, it was yesterday, because the mail had just come and I was sorting through it—I was sitting at the kitchen table, looking down at this lovely spread in *Southern Living* magazine. I’m just... normal, I suppose. \n\nAnd as for being irritable, well, I get a little frustrated sometimes, sure, but who wouldn't when they drop a whole tin of sewing buttons on the floor because their hands just won't stay still? Or when I can't get a thread through a needle because I'm rushing? But irritable in general at other people? No, not really. I'm quite content. I love seeing my grandchildren, I enjoy my garden... it's not a feeling of being unusually happy or having this grand, euphoric energy in my mind. It's really just this... physical need to be doing something. \n\nI remember telling my daughter, Susan, just last week when she came over for tea. I was up and down from the table four times before she even finished her first cup, and I said to her, \"Susan, I feel perfectly fine in my head, I'm not upset, I'm not overly excited, I just need to wipe down these baseboards right this very second.\" So, no, doctor, I wouldn't say my mood is any different than it was ten or twenty years ago. My spirits are perfectly level. It's just my body that seems to think we're running a marathon!\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your memory or thinking over this past year? For example, do you sometimes forget things you normally wouldn't, or do you find it harder to concentrate or follow conversations?\n\nPatient: Memory... well, now that you ask, no, I really haven't noticed anything out of the ordinary with my memory. I mean, goodness, at 87, you expect a little slippage here and there, don't you? My friend Helen—she's 89, bless her—she can't remember where she put her glasses half the time, and they're usually sitting right on top of her head! But me? No, my mind is sharp as a tack. I can tell you exactly what I wore to my high school graduation, and I can tell you what I had for breakfast this morning—oatmeal with half a sliced banana and just a sprinkle of cinnamon, by the way. My hearing is still quite good, thankfully. It's just that... well, sometimes when people are talking, especially if they talk very slowly or take a long time to get to the point, I just want them to hurry up! I find myself nodding along, saying \"Yes, yes, go on,\" because my hands are itching to get back to whatever project I was working on. Just yesterday, my neighbor Mr. Henderson was telling me about his new sprinkler system, and he was going into all this detail about the water pressure and the timer settings, and I understood every word of it, I really did, but I was practically bouncing on my heels because I knew I still had two dozen cookies to frost for the bake sale. I didn't lose the thread of the conversation, I just... I just wanted it to be over so I could get back to doing things! So no, my memory and my thinking are just fine. It's just this constant, buzzing need to be busy that's the problem.\n\nDoctor: Over this past year, have you noticed any changes in how you interact with people, or has anyone commented that you seem different in your personality or behavior—perhaps more impulsive, or doing things you wouldn't normally do before thinking them through?\n\nPatient: Changes in my personality? Oh, goodness me, no. Nothing like that at all. I mean, my regular doctor—Dr. Aris, he’s been my primary care physician for, oh, it must be fifteen years now, ever since Dr. Miller retired and moved down to Florida. Dr. Miller was a wonderful man, but Dr. Aris is very thorough too. Anyway, every year I go in for my physical, and I sit up there on that exam table with the crinkly paper—which I just despise, by the way, because I can't stop swinging my legs and it makes such a racket—and he does all the usual checks. \n\nHe listens to my heart, he checks my blood pressure, which is always excellent, and he does that little test where he taps your knees with the little rubber triangle hammer. But anyway, yes, looking at your nose. \n\nAnd now down at my lap. Without moving my head... okay, ready? Zip! Down they go. \n\nSee? Just my eyes. Right down to my lap.
